# Reading Logs
### How to Interprete Log File Generated by the Detector

*This manually is mostly written for Jeremy Taylor, likely the only one who will ever read this. XD*

## Help! Something Broke. (sys_logs)

If you're reading this, then something broke... sorry about that. Anyway, you came to the right place. 

Sys_logs holds exactly one log file per each time the FKW_detector is ran. Each log is titled as follows: 'main_{RPi_start_time}.log'. In the sys_log files are the full collection of print statements produced by the FKW_detector. Generally these print statements give you an idea of what program is doing what when. This should give you some insight on where your error occured. Good luck! 


IMPORTANT: This datetime is a Raspberry Pi date time, not the WISPR datetime which is used when naming the dive logs and other data products. You can correlate RPi datetimes to dive logs by checking the RPi_time=... in the dive logs. Hopefully this is not necessary because this process is tedious.

## What Happened in the Last Dive? (dive_logs) 

If you're reading this, you either didn't get your desired data product or you're curious about what took place on the previous dive. 

Dive_logs holds a collection of files each representing one dive. The dive log files are named as: '{first_file_analyzed}_{last_file_analyzed}.csv'. In each csv is the full list of all the 'new' files that the detector has not yet seen. For each file, the dive log holds the file name, start time, selected for sampling, dat to wave, wave to spectro, image analyzed. The last four of these are true / false flags. 

Only a subset of audio files are select for sampling due to the power limitations of the glider, hence the select for sampling flag gives insight on which files were chosen. The detector selects an even distribution of files from the total, ie. if there are 10 files and the max number of files to analyze is 5, the detector would select every 2nd file. Note, it takes about one minute to fully analyze one minute of audio data. 

The other flags give insight how the file went through the pipeline. In testing, most of the time if the selected for sampling for flag was true, all the other flags would be true as well. However, one file never made it past the 'wave_to_spectro' flag for some reason. 

Note: if you analyze the exact same group of files twice, the dive log will have the exact same file name, hence, the newer file will over-write the other. 

## Which Files Has the FKW_detector Seen? (analyst_logs)

Analyst logs are essential to the function of FKW_detector. Because we don't plan on analyzing every new file, we need to keep track of which files the system has seen without just looking into the 'completed' pile. 


Analyst logs is a (theoretically) sorted list of every file name in the directory-of-files-to-analyze. Every time the detector is run, it looks into the selected directory for new files, new files are passed down the chain for selection and analyzation then added to the analyst logs so they can be ignored on the next run. Hence, if you're testing on the bench with a fixed set of fils, you need to remove some of them from analyst logs each time or you'll constantly get 'no new files'.
